newsitem.title: TANZANIA: UN Rwanda crimes witness says beaten by accused.
newsitem.headline: UN Rwanda crimes witness says beaten by accused.

text.p: The United Nations Rwanda war crimes tribunal on Wednesday heard a 70-year-old Hutu woman tell how a former government official in the dock beat her to the point of death.
She said the accused Jean-Paul Akayesu, 43, the former mayor of Rwanda's central Taba commune and charged with genocide, wanted her to disclose where he could find a certain Tutsi woman.

Akayesu has pleaded not guilty to charges of genocide and crimes against humanity during the 1994 mass killings of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus. If convicted he faces life imprisonment, the tribunal's highest penalty.

The killings were sparked off by the assassination of Hutu president and military strongman Juvenal Habyarimana. Angry Habyarimana supporters took up arms and hunted down Tutsis and Hutus opposed to his junta.
During April 1994 Akayesu came to the witness' house with Interahamwe militiamen and broke down the door demanding to know where a Tutsi woman called Alexia was hiding, the witness said.
The witness, known as "N" to protect her identity, testified she was severely beaten and driven by Akayesu to a nearby mine, dragged out of the vehicle, tied up and forced to lie down.
"Akayesu got into the front of the car to turn the wheel and said: 'Lie down in front we are going to run you over," witness "N" said. She was not run over.
Later that night she was driven into a forest, tied up and beaten further: "I was almost dead from the beating I had suffered," she said, adding she could no longer work and needed help dressing.
Her testimony corroborates that given by two earlier prosecution witnesses presenting Akayesu as a sadist who used his authority as mayor to hunt down Tutsis.
She said she attended a meeting at which Akayesu said pregnant Hutu women married to Tutsis should be ripped open and their babies killed.
The old woman, who wore a long cardigan, a multi-coloured headscarf and supported herself with a stick, delivered her testimony in a headlong rush.

Akayesu is the first suspect to be tried before the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda (ICTR) set up to bring to justice the main planners of the genocide, which ended when Tutsi rebels seized power and drove the Hutus into exile.
He will have the opportunity to put questions to witness "N" when the session restarts at 11 a.m. (0800 GMT) on Thursday, said Presiding Judge Laity Kama.
The judge will rule later this week on Akayesu's earlier request to fire lawyers assigned to him after he twice dismissed previous counsel.

Akayesu, confined since last May to U.N. remand cells near the court, was reportedly happy with the court's decision to let him cross-examine witnesses and play a leading role in his own trial, sources at the court told Reuters.
Earlier witness "K", a Rwandan Tutsi accountant in Akayesu's office said she witnessed Akayesu order eight Tutsis hacked to death on April 19, 1994.
In all 21 people have been indicted by the tribunal, of whom seven are in custody at tribunal headquarters in Arusha.
Separate trials have also started in the Rwandan capital Kigali and in other towns of the tiny tea and coffee-growing central African nation.
Rwanda holds about 90,000 people suspected of taking part in the genocide but has only just started putting them on trial. Two Hutu men were sentenced to death in Rwanda on January 3.
